Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Martin had grown up in a European immigrant household in which his father’s moods set the temperature of the home as much as the weather outside. When he was a child, his caregiver’s abuse was physical, delivered in ways that taught him to brace before he understood what he was bracing for. He later described those years not with a single vivid scene but as a series of moments in which a hand, an object, or a sudden change in tone could mean pain. In adulthood he had built a steady life for himself in the United States, married, and worked for decades as a software engineer, a role that suited his preference for structure and limited personal intrusion. He was known as competent and precise, but also private, and over time he came to keep himself carefully contained.

The memories did not stay in the past in the way Martin had hoped they would. At times a memory of the abuse would come to mind suddenly, without warning, and with it the old sense that he was back in the same helpless position. He could be sitting at his desk writing code or standing in the kitchen at home when an image would flash through his mind so abruptly that he would lose his place in the room around him. He found these moments especially unsettling because they did not arrive through reflection or choice; they seemed to seize him. He also noticed that certain sensations on his skin, particularly a specific temperature, could carry him back before he had time to prepare. A cool draft on his forearm, or water that was unexpectedly cold, could make him flinch and feel unnaturally exposed, as if his body had recognized something before his thoughts could catch up. He spoke of his heart racing or pounding as another particularly difficult cue. When his pulse became noticeably strong in his chest, he would become sharply aware of it, as though the sensation itself were a warning that something was already wrong.

Over the years he had developed habits that made daily life smaller. He avoided paying attention to his own body and, as much as possible, avoided looking at it as well. He disliked mirrors not because of vanity but because turning his attention inward could make him feel trapped with sensations he did not want to register. He also began avoiding physical contact with others in a broad and practical sense. Even in his marriage he preferred that affection remain limited and predictable, and he would stiffen if his wife touched him unexpectedly. If they were out together and a hand brushed his arm from behind in a crowded aisle, he would react with alarm before he had time to recognize who it was. These reactions embarrassed him, but he experienced them as automatic and unavoidable. He also pulled away from people he had socialised with before the trauma had become so consuming. Former colleagues, old friends, and familiar acquaintances were increasingly easier to sidestep than to meet, because being with them meant being observed, expected to converse, and sometimes touched on the shoulder or back in greeting. Gradually, he let invitations go unanswered and kept his world organized around routines that reduced contact.

At work, Martin’s environment also fed his sense of alertness. As a software engineer he spent long hours in offices and, more recently, in spaces where tools, cords, and sharp office equipment were part of the background. He noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in almost any setting, not in a dramatic or paranoid way, but with a reflexive scan of what could be used to harm him if something went wrong. He would register a heavy metal object on a desk, a box cutter in a drawer, or even an ordinary household utensil with an attention that felt hard to turn off. He described it as a kind of constant caution: he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. That conviction left him feeling like an outsider, even in rooms where nothing was happening. He had the sense that other people moved through life assuming basic safety, while he remained on the edge of things, never fully part of the group and never fully able to relax into trust. People, in his view, could not be trusted; his own body, he felt, reacted to danger before he had even had time to think.

By the time he sought help, Martin had spent years organizing his life around keeping distance, staying alert, and not being surprised. The pattern had narrowed his social world and made him more isolated at work and at home, even though he and his wife remained together and he continued to function in his job. What finally brought him in was the growing discomfort of living so permanently on guard that even ordinary moments felt effortful. He wanted to understand why a racing heart, an unexpected touch, or a cold sensation on his skin could still move him so quickly into alarm. More than anything, he hoped for some way to live without feeling that danger could emerge at any moment and without the burden of believing he would always remain on the outside looking in.
